narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 72.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—roughly a seven-in-ten risk. In this admission process, that high failure risk was treated as too large to admit.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing. Your third-year decile was 1, compared with an average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this factor pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The next most important factor was your LSAT score: 23.5 versus an accepted-student average of 37.18, which also pushed toward failure. Third was your undergraduate GPA of 2.60, below the accepted average of 3.23; in this prediction it was the only leading factor that leaned toward passing, but its influence was smaller than the other two and could not outweigh them. Gender and race were not used.

To improve future chances, focus on the clearest academic signals: prepare for a higher LSAT score, strengthen your academic record where possible, and seek advising about bar-exam readiness and any available remedial or support programs before reapplying.
